newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Strong cocoa market plays into hands of shippers.
newsitem.headline: Strong cocoa market plays into hands of shippers.

text.p: Ivorian cocoa shippers are continuing to cash in on a strong futures market and a favourable French franc/sterling exchange rate to unwind long physical positions, European traders said on Friday.
"The shippers are running the physical market at the moment," one trader said.
Another factor of the recent price rally, in which benchmark futures rose to a seven-month high of 1,048 stg a tonne last week, had been the active participation of industry.
"Industry usually sit on their hands during a rally like this but they've been in buying cover," another said.
The key May contract on Friday was trading up six stg at 1,037, with traders citing origin selling as capping the market.
Traders said industry's cover had been running at between eight and nine months but this had increased over the past week as jitters caused some protection buying.

Fears were mounting over the potential sway U.S. trade house Phibro might have over the market by using the estimated 300,000 tonnes of cocoa it is believed to have stockpiled from the London exchange in September.
"If Phibro does something with May or Sept (futures) then there could be a lot less cocoa around and industry has felt the need to take on some extra protection," one said.
Some of those concerns seemed to be confirmed last week when Phibro director Anthony Ward said he expected cocoa prices to hit 1,500 stg a tonne by the summer.
Other worries in the market were continued dry weather in Ivory Coast and talk of a smaller than normal bean size in the Ivorian mid-crop.
Active Ivorian shipper selling had made a marked impact on the way physical differentials had been quoted, with one trader saying a two-tier market was now in effect.

Shippers who had been issued with export contracts that were initially above the market were now more than happy to sell into the rally and take their profits. This had led to nearby Ivory Coast cocoa being sold for 40 stg or more under May in some cases.
However, if a buyer weny to a regular European trade house, the price was a more standard 30 stg under, traders said.
"The idea of a diffential is of little consequence any more. It no longer represents the difference between the origin price and what industry wants to pay," a trader said.

Other origins on offer in Europe included Ghana, which had unusually been selling a variety of positions as far out as into 1998. Dealers said differentials were fluctuating up to 10 stg either side of the terminal market.
Indonesia had also been an aggressive seller of beans and products, although mostly for customers in the U.S.
Traders said Indonesian beans were quoted around $150 below the New York market.

Stocks of cocoa in Amsterdam had continued to swell on high shipments from Ivory Coast. The latest data from warehouse firm SGS Europe showed stocks had grown to 572,000 tonnes by the start of this month, up 56,000 on a month earlier.
